evergreen_facts.text: Seoul, then called Hanyang, became the capital of Korea's Joseon dynasty in 1394 under King Taejo.
King Sejong the Great proclaimed Hangul, the Korean alphabet, from his court in Seoul in 1446.
Seoul's Fortress Wall, first built in 1396, once ran along the four mountains around the old capital.
Gyeongbokgung, built in 1395, was the main royal palace of the Joseon dynasty in Seoul.
Changdeokgung Palace in Seoul is a UNESCO World Heritage Site admired for blending into its wooded setting.
Jongmyo Shrine in Seoul, where Joseon kings and queens are honored in ancestral rites, is UNESCO-listed.
N Seoul Tower stands on top of Namsan, a mountain in the middle of Seoul with views across the city.
The Han River flows west through Seoul, splitting the city into northern and southern halves.
Seoul is ringed by mountains, and Bukhansan National Park reaches into the city's northern edge.
Seoul hosted the 1988 Summer Olympics, the second Olympic Games ever held in Asia.
Kukkiwon in Seoul is the world headquarters of taekwondo, the Korean martial art known for its kicks.
Kimchi, spicy fermented napa cabbage or radish, is served as a side dish at nearly every meal in Seoul.
Seoul's Gwangjang Market, opened in 1905, is famous for street food such as bindaetteok mung bean pancakes.
Kimjang, the communal autumn making of kimchi in Korea, is on UNESCO's list of intangible heritage.
Seoul's Bukchon Hanok Village preserves hundreds of hanok, traditional Korean houses with tiled roofs.
Cheonggyecheon, a stream in downtown Seoul, was restored in 2005 after decades buried under an elevated road.
